Mapping Burn Severity of Colorado's Two Largest Wildfires

Max Warnock | October 2026

This project maps burn severity for the 2020 Cameron Peak and East Troublesome fires with satellite imagery, and looks at the watersheds, vegetation recovery, and homes affected.

Background: burn severity map of the East Troublesome Fire

The 2020 fires¶

In 2020, Colorado had the two largest wildfires in its history. The Cameron Peak Fire started on August 13 in the mountains west of Fort Collins and burned 208,913 acres. The East Troublesome Fire started on October 14 in Grand County and burned 193,694 acres.

Cameron Peak burned for almost four months and East Troublesome for about seven weeks (Butzer, 2020; Miller, 2020). Not every part of a fire burns the same. Some areas only lose their grass and shrubs, while others lose entire forests. This project maps how severely each part of the two fires burned, and answers three questions:

  1. Where did the fires burn most severely, by watershed?
  2. How has vegetation recovered from 2021 to 2026?
  3. How much of the high severity area is in or near homes in the wildland urban interface (WUI)?

Mapping burn severity¶

The project uses NASA's Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2 (HLS) imagery, which combines the Landsat 8/9 and Sentinel-2 satellites into one 30m dataset. For every summer from 2019 to 2026, the clear images from June 1 to September 30 were combined into one median image for each fire (Howe et al., 2022; Parks et al., 2018).

Burn severity was mapped with the differenced Normalized Burn Ratio (dNBR). NBR is high for healthy vegetation and low for burned land, so the drop in NBR from the summer before the fires (2019) to the summer after (2021) shows how severely each 30m pixel burned:

$$ \text{NBR} = \frac{\text{NIR} - \text{SWIR2}}{\text{NIR} + \text{SWIR2}} \qquad \text{dNBR} = (\text{NBR}_{2019} - \text{NBR}_{2021}) \times 1000 $$

dNBR was then split into burn severity classes with the Key and Benson (2006) thresholds, a standard made for the USDA Forest Service's FIREMON program that uses the same thresholds for every fire.

The project is split into six notebooks:

Notebook What it does
01_data_download Downloads the fire perimeters, MTBS maps, watersheds, WUI map, and HLS summer images
02_burn_severity Maps dNBR and the Key and Benson burn severity classes
03_mtbs_comparison Compares the burn severity map with the official MTBS maps
04_watershed_severity Finds the high severity area in each subwatershed
05_vegetation_recovery Tracks the vegetation in each burn severity class from 2021 to 2026
06_wui_severity Finds the high severity area in and near the WUI

Burn severity¶

About a quarter of Cameron Peak (52,930 acres) and a fifth of East Troublesome (35,738 acres) burned at high severity. Another 26% of Cameron Peak and 31% of East Troublesome burned at moderate-high severity.

To check the map, it was compared with the official Monitoring Trends in Burn Severity (MTBS) maps (Eidenshink et al., 2007). The two maps agree on about 70% of the burned area. The Key and Benson map has less high severity than MTBS, but 92-96% of what it calls high is also high in MTBS, so its high severity areas are a conservative estimate.

Where did the fires burn most severely?¶

The burned area was split into HUC12 subwatersheds, the smallest watersheds in the USGS Watershed Boundary Dataset. Seven subwatersheds had 20% or more of their area burn at high severity:

  • Cameron Peak: Little Beaver Creek (40%), Miller Fork (37%), Sheep Creek (33%), Upper Buckhorn Creek (28%), and Hague Creek (22%), in the Cache la Poudre and Big Thompson river basins
  • East Troublesome: Headwaters Willow Creek (32%) and Onahu Creek-Colorado River (27%), in the Colorado River headwaters

High severity areas lose the most ground cover, so these subwatersheds are the most at risk of erosion after the fires.

How has the vegetation recovered?¶

Recovery was tracked with summer NDVI, a measure of how green the land is (Tucker, 1979). Each burned area was compared with unburned land outside the fires in the same summer, so a wet or dry summer isn't mistaken for recovery.

By 2026, the moderate-high and high severity areas had regained about 40-45% of the greenness they lost. Most of it came back in the first three summers, and it has been slower since 2024. The high severity areas were the greenest before the fires, likely dense forest, and are now about as green as the moderate areas.

NDVI only measures greenness. Grass and shrubs can green up in a few years, but burned forest takes decades to grow back, so the forest is further from recovery than these numbers suggest.

How much high severity burn was near homes?¶

The burn severity map was compared with a 2019 WUI map from my WUI Mapping Tool, which follows the WUI definition of Radeloff et al. (2005). The WUI is land where homes are mixed into wildland vegetation (intermix) or next to it (interface).

Very little of the high severity area was in the WUI itself: 374 acres at Cameron Peak and 80 acres at East Troublesome, less than 1% of each fire's high severity area. The WUI burned much less severely than the land around it, likely because homes are mostly in valleys and clearings with less dense forest.

Fire can still reach homes from outside the WUI, because embers can fly about 2.4km ahead of a fire (Radeloff et al., 2005). 28% of the high severity area at Cameron Peak and 14% at East Troublesome was within 2.4km of the WUI, mostly along Buckhorn Creek and the Cache la Poudre River at Cameron Peak, and in the Onahu Creek-Colorado River subwatershed at East Troublesome.

Conclusion¶

Together, the two fires burned about 88,700 acres at high severity. The worst of it was in a few subwatersheds of the Cache la Poudre, Big Thompson, and Colorado rivers, and after five summers these areas have regained less than half of their lost greenness. Very little high severity fire was in the WUI, but almost a quarter of it burned close enough for embers to reach homes.

Limitations¶

  • The Key and Benson map has less high severity than MTBS, so the high severity areas in this project are on the low side
  • Burn severity was mapped from satellite imagery and wasn't checked with field plots
  • NDVI shows how green the land is, not whether the forest has grown back
  • The WUI map has 250m pixels and is from 2019. Burn severity measures the vegetation, not damage to homes, so this project doesn't show which homes burned
